title: When the Parish Burns
premise: August Oyelaran, an insurance investigator whose photographic memory has made him the quiet keeper of his coastal parish's secrets, receives a confession letter postmarked the day after old Father Brennan's funeral—signed by a man who drowned thirty years ago. The letter names three townspeople and a fire that was never reported, forcing August to reopen a case he helped bury as a teenager. As he cross-examines alibis woven decades ago, he realizes his own memory holds the missing piece: what he saw on the pier the night the parish hall burned. The tide eventually gives up the truth—that the priest himself set the fire to cover a theft, and the 'drowned' man fled with the evidence—leaving August to decide whether inheritance means protecting the town's lies or finally letting them burn.
about_author: Jonah Reyes is a former claims adjuster from the Gulf Coast who spent eleven years reading other people's disasters before writing his own. He lives in a converted boathouse and insists he remembers everything, which is why he writes fiction.

chapters.title: Postmarked Yesterday
chapters.summary: August Oyelaran, POV. Days after Father Brennan's funeral, August sorts the priest's mail and finds a confession letter dated the day after the death—signed by Tomas Reyes, drowned in 1994. The letter references a fire and three names August knows intimately. Emotional beat: the chill of realizing his carefully alphabetized world has a file he never created.

chapters.title: The Alphabet of Small Towns
chapters.summary: August's POV, flashback-laced. He reconstructs the 1994 parish hall fire from memory: no police report, insurance denied on a technicality he himself drafted. He visits the first named person, widow Delphine Marsh, whose alibi is word-for-word identical to one she gave thirty years ago. Emotional beat: dread that memory is both his gift and his trap.

chapters.title: What Delphine Kept
chapters.summary: Delphine's POV. She recalls the night of the fire—her husband's absence, the priest's strange calm, a second set of footprints on the pier. She lies to August gently, the way she has lied for decades. Emotional beat: tenderness curdled into complicity; she recognizes in August the boy who saw too much.

chapters.title: Low Tide, Old Bones
chapters.summary: August's POV. A storm uncovers debris in the cove: a melted strongbox matching the parish's missing collection records. Someone else has been searching recently—boot prints too fresh for the tide. Emotional beat: the case shifts from paper mystery to physical danger; someone alive wants the past to stay submerged.

chapters.title: The Second Name
chapters.summary: August's POV. He confronts Councilman Harlan Voss, the second name, whose alibi places him at a banquet that—August remembers precisely—was cancelled that night. Voss threatens August's job, revealing the insurer was pressured to deny the claim. Emotional beat: anger hardening into resolve; the machinery of silence had authors.

chapters.title: Interference Pattern
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: August and his estranged sister Grace, a nurse who left town after their mother's death. Grace remembers the summer of 1994 differently—and better. Their argument over memory versus mercy mirrors the town's larger fracture. Emotional beat: grief that survival required forgetting, and love that requires remembering.

chapters.title: The Third Name Is His Own
chapters.summary: August's POV, devastating turn. Cross-referencing the letter's phrasing against his own childhood statement to the insurer, he realizes the handwriting analysis points somewhere impossible: the confession echoes words he spoke at sixteen. The third name was redacted—by him. Emotional beat: vertigo; the archivist discovers he is also an exhibit.

chapters.title: Firewall
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. Panicked, Voss burns Delphine's letters and hires someone to search August's office. We learn Voss witnessed the priest's theft but stayed silent in exchange for the council seat. Emotional beat: cowardice rationalized as stewardship; the antagonist becomes pitiable without becoming innocent.

chapters.title: The Tide Gives Up What It Took
chapters.summary: August's POV, climax. Lured to the pier at night by a forged note, August faces Voss's hired man—but Grace arrives, having decoded her brother's files. In the confrontation, August's total recall reconstructs the full night: the priest set the fire; Tomas took the ledger and ran; young August saw it all and traded silence for the town's protection. Emotional beat: the past arriving all at once, unalphabetized.

chapters.title: Everything Must Be Filed Somewhere
chapters.summary: August's POV, resolution. Voss confesses publicly rather than face exposure; the ledger surfaces, clearing Tomas's name and disgracing the beloved priest. August donates the parish records to the county archive—memory shared instead of hoarded—and reconciles haltingly with Grace. Final image: the tide coming in clean. Emotional beat: inheritance redefined—not the secrets we keep, but the truths we hand on.
